cases.audioScript: On February 13th, 2017, two best friends, thirteen-year-old Abby Williams and fourteen-year-old Libby German, went for a walk on the Monon High Bridge Trail in Delphi, Indiana. They never came home. The next day, searchers found both girls near the trail. Libby had used her phone to record a man on the bridge, and that recording, with a few chilling words, became one of the most recognized pieces of evidence in Indiana history. For years, the case stayed unsolved, and the man in the video was known only as Bridge Guy. In October 2022, Indiana State Police arrested Richard Allen of Delphi. In November 2024, a jury found him guilty of murder, and in December he was sentenced to one hundred thirty years in prison, the maximum. Prosecutors credited Libby for having the courage to record, and Abby for hiding the phone so investigators could find it. Allen's conviction is now under appeal, and the Indiana Court of Appeals heard arguments in September 2026. Abby and Libby are remembered by their families and by a community that put up orange porch lights in their memory. Their families and neighbors have also worked to build a memorial park for them near Delphi.
cases.summary: Abby Williams (13) and Libby German (14) were dropped off near the Monon High Bridge Trail outside Delphi on the afternoon of Feb 13, 2017 and did not return. Their bodies were found the next day about half a mile east of the bridge. Libby had recorded video and audio on her phone of a man walking toward them; police released a still image, then audio of the man saying 'Down the hill.' The man was nicknamed 'Bridge Guy.' Years of tips and releases followed, including a new sketch in 2019. In 2022 investigators found a misfiled tip about Richard Allen. He was arrested Oct 26, 2022 and charged with murder. After a trial that opened Oct 18, 2024, a jury found him guilty in November 2024, and Judge Fran Gull sentenced him to 130 years on Dec 20, 2024, vacating duplicate felony-murder counts. The Indiana Court of Appeals heard his appeal Sept 21, 2026; a decision is pending as of the sources checked.
cases.solvedHow: A tip naming Richard Allen from 2017 had been misfiled; a volunteer file clerk's review in 2022 led investigators back to him. Prosecutors then tied him to the case through phone video, the unspent bullet, vehicle evidence, witness accounts and his own statements.
cases.techniques: Tip-line review (misfiled 2017 tip rediscovered in Sept 2022); Digital forensics on the victim's phone (video/audio); Firearms/ballistics comparison of an unspent round; Surveillance video and vehicle registration records; Witness and custodial statements

cases.audioScript: On Good Friday, April first, 1988, eight-year-old April Tinsley was playing with friends in Fort Wayne, Indiana. She went to get her umbrella, and she never came home. Three days later, a jogger found her body in a ditch near Spencerville. For thirty years, her killer was a mystery. Beginning in 1990, someone left chilling notes around Fort Wayne, bragging about the crime and threatening other children. Investigators saved the DNA from those notes and from the scene, and in 2015 and 2016 they released composite sketches built from that DNA. Then, in 2018, detectives sent the profile to a genetic genealogy company. Genealogist CeCe Moore used a public DNA database to trace the profile to two brothers. Detectives collected a discarded sample, the DNA matched, and on July 15th, 2018, they arrested John Miller of Grabill. He confessed, pleaded guilty that December, and was sentenced to eighty years. April's case became one of the early cold cases in America solved with this technique. April was eight years old, a choir member and a second-grader, and her community never stopped saying her name.
cases.summary: April Tinsley was abducted in Fort Wayne on April 1, 1988 and found dead April 4 in a ditch west of Spencerville. Between 1990 and 2004 an anonymous person left notes in the Fort Wayne area claiming responsibility and threatening more crimes; DNA on items left with the 2004 notes matched the crime-scene profile. In 2015 Parabon NanoLabs produced a DNA 'Snapshot' composite; in May 2018 a Fort Wayne detective submitted the DNA for genetic genealogy. CeCe Moore used GEDmatch to narrow the family to two brothers by July 2, 2018. Detectives confirmed a match using DNA from discarded trash, approached John D. Miller on July 15, 2018, and he confessed. Charged with murder, child molestation and confinement, he pleaded not guilty July 19, pleaded guilty Dec 7, 2018, and was sentenced Dec 21, 2018 to 80 years.
cases.solvedHow: Forensic genetic genealogy: the crime-scene DNA profile was uploaded to GEDmatch by Parabon NanoLabs; genealogist CeCe Moore built family trees to identify two brothers, and a covert DNA comparison confirmed the match.
cases.techniques: Forensic genetic genealogy (GEDmatch / Parabon NanoLabs); DNA phenotyping composite sketch (2015, updated 2016); Covert DNA sample from discarded trash for confirmation; Linkage of 1990-2004 taunting notes by DNA

cases.audioScript: On the evening of Friday, July seventh, 1972, twenty-six-year-old Phyllis Bailer left Indianapolis with her three-year-old daughter, headed for Bluffton to visit her parents. They never arrived. The next morning, Phyllis's car was found abandoned on Interstate 69 in Grant County, hood up. About an hour later, a woman driving in Allen County found Phyllis in a ditch beside a country road. Her little girl was alive and unharmed. Phyllis had been shot and sexually assaulted. In 1972, DNA testing didn't exist. Over the years, a partial DNA profile was developed from her clothing, and in 2024 the Indiana State Police lab produced a much stronger one. Working with a forensic genealogy company in California, the ISP Cold Case Unit identified the killer in early 2025: Fred Lienemann, a man with a long criminal record and no known connection to Phyllis. He had been murdered in Detroit in 1985, so he could never be tried. State police said that if he were alive, he would have been charged. For Phyllis's family, after fifty-three years, there are finally answers.
cases.summary: Phyllis Bailer, 26, left Indianapolis around 8 p.m. on July 7, 1972, with her 3-year-old daughter, bound for Bluffton. Her car was found abandoned northbound on I-69 in Grant County the next morning. About an hour later a driver near West and Shoaff Roads in Allen County found Phyllis dead and her daughter unharmed. The autopsy found a gunshot wound and sexual assault. A partial DNA profile was developed from her clothing in later years; in 2024 ISP's lab developed a stronger profile and, with Identifinders International, genealogists identified Fred Allen Lienemann in early 2025. He had a long criminal history and was murdered in Detroit in 1985. ISP announced the finding April 16, 2025, stating he would have been charged by the Allen County Prosecutor had he been alive.
cases.solvedHow: ISP's Cold Case Unit re-tested clothing as DNA technology improved, then partnered with Identifinders International to run forensic genetic genealogy, identifying the DNA contributor as Fred Allen Lienemann.
cases.techniques: Re-testing of preserved clothing with newer DNA methods; Forensic genetic genealogy (Identifinders International); Criminal-history and death records review

cases.audioScript: On the night of August sixth, 1975, seventeen-year-old Laurel Jean Mitchell finished her shift at a snack bar at the Epworth Forest church camp in North Webster, Indiana. She set off on foot to meet friends at a nearby amusement park, and she was never seen alive again. The next morning, two fishermen found her body in the Elkhart River, many miles away. The autopsy showed she had fought hard to survive. Her clothing and belongings were saved, and for nearly fifty years, investigators kept working. New DNA testing on that clothing, and tips from people who said they'd heard boasts about the crime, led Indiana State Police to two men. In February 2023, Fred Bandy Junior and John Lehman were arrested. In October 2024, a judge found Bandy guilty of first-degree murder and sentenced him to life in prison. Lehman received eight years for conspiracy. Laurel's sister said she felt relief, after a long road. Laurel was a dancer, a friend, and a daughter whose parents never learned what happened. Forty-nine years later, her family finally has an answer.
cases.summary: Laurel Jean Mitchell, 17, was dropped off at the Epworth Forest church camp snack bar on Aug 6, 1975. Around 10 p.m. she was seen walking toward Adventureland Amusement Park and was not seen again. A missing-person report was filed at 4:16 a.m. Aug 7 and her body was found at 10:30 a.m. in the Elkhart River near the Mallard Roost access. The autopsy found drowning and signs of a violent struggle. Her clothing was preserved. Tips in 2013, 2014 and 2019 described admissions by two men; resubmitted clothing yielded a male DNA profile (certificate Feb 2020). A voluntary DNA sample from Bandy in Dec 2022 produced a Jan 2023 result stating he was 13 billion times more likely than an unknown person to be the contributor. ISP and the Noble County Sheriff arrested Bandy and Lehman on Feb 6, 2023. Lehman was sentenced to 8 years (Oct 11, 2024). Bandy was convicted in a bench trial Oct 7, 2024, received life on Oct 22, 2024, and the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld the conviction in July 2025.
cases.solvedHow: Preserved clothing was re-tested with modern DNA methods, and long-standing tips about admissions pointed investigators to two men; a voluntary DNA sample matched the profile and arrests followed.
cases.techniques: Long-term evidence preservation; Modern STR DNA testing (ISP Laboratory Division); Voluntary DNA sample comparison; Cold-case tip development (2013-2019); Vehicle records review

cases.audioScript: Between 1987 and 1990, a killer moved along Interstate 65, striking at night-shift motel clerks. In February 1987, Vicki Heath was murdered at a Super 8 in Elizabethtown, Kentucky. On March third, 1989, Peggy Gill was killed at the Days Inn in Merrillville, Indiana, and the same night, Jeanne Gilbert was taken from the Days Inn in Remington. In January 1990, another clerk in Columbus, Indiana, was attacked, but she survived and gave police an excellent description. For more than thirty years, detectives chased leads across the country. Ballistics linked the Indiana murders, and DNA linked the others. In 2019, Indiana State Police asked the FBI for help, and investigators used investigative genetic genealogy. A close relative's DNA led to Harry Edward Greenwell, who died in 2013. In April 2022, police announced that Greenwell was responsible. He was never charged, but for the families of Vicki, Peggy, and Jeanne, and for the survivor, the question of who was finally had an answer. Jeanne's daughter said her family was grateful to every agency that never gave up.
cases.summary: Vicki Heath (41) was murdered Feb 21, 1987 at a Super 8 in Elizabethtown, Kentucky. On March 3, 1989, Peggy Gill (24) was murdered at the Days Inn in Merrillville, and Jeanne Gilbert (34) was abducted from the Days Inn in Remington and found dead near Brookston. On Jan 2, 1990 a clerk at the Days Inn in Columbus, Indiana was sexually assaulted and stabbed but escaped. ISP lab work matched ballistic evidence in the Gill and Gilbert killings and DNA linking the Heath and Gilbert murders to the Columbus assault. In 2019 ISP requested FBI GRIT help; investigative genealogy matched a close relative of Harry Edward Greenwell (born Dec 9, 1944; died January 2013 in New Albin, Iowa) with >99% probability. ISP and FBI announced the result April 5, 2022; investigators believe Greenwell may be responsible for additional crimes along I-65 from Gary to Mobile, Alabama (ISP spokesperson, ABC).

cases.audioScript: Andi Wagner was twenty-four years old when her family last heard from her. On August sixth, 2022, she left her family's home in Evansville, Indiana, with an overnight bag. She called her mother in Texas about possibly moving away, and she spoke briefly with her sister. Then the calls stopped. Her family reported her missing on August twelfth. Andi had been struggling with addiction, but those who love her say she was working hard to get better, and she had planned to join her mother in Texas. Her mother, Elane, moved to Evansville to search for her daughter, and she passed away in December 2023 without answers. In May 2024, Evansville police, state police, and the FBI searched three locations in and near Oakland City after a tip. Nothing has been announced publicly since. A twenty-five-thousand-dollar reward is being offered. Andi has brown hair and brown eyes and several tattoos. If you know anything, please contact the Evansville Police Department or the FBI. Andi's family says it is time for her to come home.

cases.audioScript: Lauren Spierer was a twenty-year-old Indiana University student from Scarsdale, New York. In the early hours of June third, 2011, she spent the night out in Bloomington with friends, including time at Kilroy's Sports Bar. Around four-thirty that morning, she was last seen walking south near North College Avenue and West Eleventh Street, headed toward her apartment. She never arrived. Over the following days and years, searchers combed lakes, forests, and fields, and the FBI searched a property in Morgan County in 2015. No definitive evidence has ever been found. Her parents believe she is no longer alive and have offered a substantial reward. In June 2026, fifteen years later, the Bloomington Police Department said the case is still very active, with twenty-three new tips in the past year leading to multiple interviews. Lauren's family says it will never stop searching for answers. If you have any information, no matter how small it may seem, contact the Bloomington Police Department or visit findlauren dot com. Lauren is remembered for her smile, her energy, and her zest for life, and she is still missing.

cases.audioScript: On Friday, November seventeenth, 1978, four young employees were closing the Burger Chef restaurant on Crawfordsville Road in Speedway, Indiana. Jayne Friedt, twenty, the assistant manager, and three teenagers, Ruth Shelton, Daniel Davis, and Mark Flemmonds, were working that night. Just after midnight, a coworker stopped by and found the back door open, the manager's office in disarray, and the staff gone. About five hundred eighty dollars had been taken. On Sunday, the bodies of all four were found in a wooded area in Johnson County. For decades, detectives followed leads across the country. Investigators say the early scene was not preserved the way it would be today, and the restaurant reopened soon afterward. Indiana State Police now say they are focused on a group of people who were committing restaurant robberies at the time. A reward was offered then, and the case has drawn books, podcasts, and documentaries. No one has ever been charged. The four were young workers just doing their jobs. State police are still asking anyone with information to come forward. The families have waited more than forty-eight years for answers.
cases.summary: Four Burger Chef employees were abducted from the Speedway restaurant at 5725 Crawfordsville Road between about 11 p.m. Nov 17, 1978 and midnight; $581 was taken. An off-duty employee found the back door open just after midnight. Jayne Friedt's car was found near the Speedway Police Department. On Nov 19 the bodies were found in rural Johnson County: two had been shot with a .38-caliber firearm, one had been stabbed, and one died of head injuries. Burger Chef Systems offered a $25,000 reward. The scene was cleaned and the restaurant reopened without photographs, an officer later admitted (Wikipedia). In 1984 an inmate gave a confession that he later recanted; it did not lead to charges (Wikipedia). ISP says it has focused on a group of people committing restaurant robberies at the time. The case has been the subject of books, podcasts and documentaries including 'The Speedway Murders' (2024).

cases.audioScript: In the spring of 1992, a killer drove west along Interstate 70, striking small stores where employees were working alone. On April eighth, twenty-six-year-old Robin Fuldauer was shot while working at a Payless shoe store on Pendleton Pike in Indianapolis. Three days later, Patricia Smith and Patricia Magers were killed at a bridal shop in Wichita, Kansas. On April twenty-seventh, Michael McCown was killed in his mother's ceramics shop in Terre Haute, Indiana. On May third, Nancy Kitzmiller was killed at a shoe store in St. Charles, Missouri, and on May seventh, Sarah Blessing was killed at her shop in Raytown, Missouri. Ballistics showed the same twenty-two-caliber pistol was used in all six killings. Little money was taken, and investigators believe the killer was targeting petite women with long brown hair; McCown was likely mistaken for a woman. Composite sketches were released, and in 2021, age-progressed versions. St. Charles police are offering a twenty-five-thousand-dollar reward, and say they have never given up. The case has no named suspect, and the six victims are remembered by their families.
cases.summary: Six people working in small stores were shot in the back of the head between April 8 and May 7, 1992 in Indianapolis, Wichita, Terre Haute, St. Charles and Raytown. Ballistics linked the killings to the same .22-caliber pistol; police believe an Erma Werke ET22 or similar. Little cash was taken and investigators doubt robbery was the primary motive. Composite sketches were produced and age-progressed images released in 2021 (Wikipedia). A $25,000 reward is offered via St. Charles police. Possible links to two Texas killings (1993) and a 2001 Terre Haute murder were investigated; none confirmed. Several suspects were ruled out. No suspect has been publicly named.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of January eighteenth, 1973, twenty-six-year-old Ann Kline was grading papers at the Old Vanderburgh County Courthouse in Evansville, Indiana. Ann was a math teacher at Lockyear College across the street, and a fire at the school had temporarily moved her class into the courthouse basement. Around three o'clock, a student stopped by to ask about a grade. A few minutes later, someone heard screaming. Ann was found in the basement hallway, fatally stabbed. Police say she was not robbed, which suggests she may have known her attacker, and they believe there may have been more than one person involved. The weapon was never found. Detectives have worked the case for over fifty years, and around 2008 said they had a break, but no one has been charged. Ann's sister Jane spoke publicly for the first time in 2024, hoping for justice. She remembers Ann as playful and full of life. Evansville police say the case remains open and active. If you know anything, call the Evansville Police Detective Unit at eight one two, four three six, seven nine seven nine.
cases.summary: Ann Kline, 26, was killed on Jan 18, 1973 in the basement level of the Old Vanderburgh County Courthouse, where her class had been temporarily relocated after a fire at nearby Lockyear College. A student who also worked as a custodian visited her classroom around 3 p.m., then heard screaming minutes later and found her. She was fatally stabbed; her purse and belongings were not taken. The knife was never found. EPD says several persons of interest were ruled out. In 2009 and 2013 14 News and NBC reported that a former lead detective was confident about an unnamed suspect and wanted to take the case to the prosecutor, but no charges followed. Detective Dillon Powers told Dateline in 2024 the case remains open and under active investigation. The Deck (audiochuck) featured the case as the 8 of Hearts.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of Friday, August seventeenth, 1984, twenty-eight-year-old Darlene Hulse was getting her three young daughters ready for the day at her home near Argos, Indiana. Around nine-thirty, a man knocked at the door. Witnesses described him as white, in his twenties, with combed-over blond hair, clean shaven, with a long face and a long nose. He forced his way in. Darlene told her two older daughters to run, and they ran to their grandparents' house for help. When officers arrived, Darlene was gone. The next day, a timber surveyor found her body in a wooded area about six miles west of her home. The man was seen driving a rusty, greenish, seventies-style four-door car, possibly a Pontiac or Oldsmobile, which has never been found. Investigators have a partial male DNA profile from her clothing. The Indiana State Police Cold Case Unit continues to investigate, and her daughters and the podcast The Deck Investigates have called for more testing. If you know anything, contact the Indiana State Police cold case hotline. Darlene's family has waited more than forty years.
cases.summary: On Aug 17, 1984, a man knocked at Darlene Hulse's rural home near Argos around 9:30 a.m., forced his way in and attacked her; two daughters escaped to relatives while the youngest, an infant, was left unharmed. Her body was found Aug 18 by a timber surveyor in woods off Olive Trail about six miles west; the autopsy ruled it a homicide by blunt-force trauma. cases.audioScript: On the morning of October third, 1970, ten-year-old Jerry Michael Bayles, known as Mike, set out before dawn to deliver the Indianapolis Star on the city's west side. He was filling in on his older brother's paper route. Around five o'clock, after only a couple of papers had been delivered, Mike vanished near South Harris Street. His bicycle was found left behind. Within hours, a farmer found Mike's body in rural western Henry County, north of Knightstown. He had been stabbed. A man was arrested early in the investigation but was not indicted, and no one has ever been charged. In 2015, a new tip brought the case back into the news, and Indiana State Police said they were working to confirm it, but the man named in that tip has died and little physical evidence remains. More than fifty years later, the Indiana State Police Pendleton District still lists Mike's murder as an open cold case. If you know anything, even something small that you have carried for decades, investigators want to hear it. Mike was a shy, smiling boy, and his friends still remember him.
cases.summary: Jerry Michael 'Mike' Bayles Jr., 10, was abducted at about 5 a.m. on Saturday, Oct 3, 1970, while delivering the Indianapolis Star on South Harris Street on Indianapolis's west side; his bicycle was found on the street. A witness reported seeing a man force a boy into a car at knifepoint (WIBC). An early suspect was arrested but not indicted by a grand jury (WTHR; WIBC). In 2015, a woman told police her late father - a man who had claimed to witness the abduction - was responsible; ISP said it was trying to confirm the account, but the man is dead and little physical evidence remains. cases.audioScript: In August 1972, twenty-five-year-old Vickie Lynn Harrell was living in Bloomington, Indiana. On August twelfth, she was seen getting into her dark blue 1965 Plymouth Valiant in a K-Mart parking lot on the east side of town. The next day, her roommate reported her missing to Bloomington police. On August fourteenth, two things happened. Her car turned up in a parking lot near the College Mall, and her body was found in neighboring Owen County, on an access road to McCormick's Creek State Park, about two and a half miles east of Spencer. Indiana State Police say she had been strangled. More than fifty years later, no one has been charged, and the Indiana State Police Bloomington District still lists her case as an open cold case. Vickie's case has drawn renewed attention from podcasters and local reporters, but the key question remains: who did she meet after leaving that parking lot? If you lived in Bloomington or Owen County in the summer of 1972 and remember anything about Vickie or her blue Valiant, the Indiana State Police want to hear from you.

cases.audioScript: In October 1974, nineteen-year-old Debra Ann Wilhite was a young mother of two, working evening shifts as a server at the Windmill, a truck-stop restaurant near U.S. 41 and State Road 57 north of Evansville. Near the end of her shift on October sixteenth, a man came in, wet from the rain, asking for a ride. Debra was last seen speaking with him, and then she left in her green 1966 Ford Galaxie. Neither Debra nor her car has ever been found. Because she was not reported missing right away, precious time was lost. Over the years, investigators have followed rumors about ponds and old strip pits, and in 2025 a volunteer dive team, working with her family, used sonar to search a wildlife area in Warrick County. They found nothing there, but planned to check more waterways between Evansville and Princeton. The Indiana State Police still list Debra's disappearance as an open case. Her daughter has spent her life searching for answers. If you remember a green Ford Galaxie with Indiana plate 26B2953, please call the Indiana State Police.

cases.audioScript: On Monday morning, September twelfth, 1977, twenty-year-old Ann Harmeier left her hometown of Cambridge City, Indiana, to drive back to Indiana University in Bloomington. She was a junior and a theater major, and she had a ten-thirty class she never missed. Her rust-colored 1971 Pontiac LeMans overheated and broke down on State Road 37, about two miles north of Martinsville. That night her mother and a friend, retracing her route, found the car on the shoulder, locked, with the hazard lights flashing and her laundry and books still inside. Ann was gone. State police and the Morgan County Sheriff set up road checks and stopped drivers to ask what they had seen. Thirty-six days later, a farmer found Ann's body in a cornfield about seven miles northeast of Martinsville. She had been strangled. Evidence from the scene was preserved and has been tested for DNA, with no match so far. Today, her cousin runs a social media campaign telling the story in Ann's own voice, hoping someone finally talks. Indiana State Police say the case remains under investigation.

Her mother and a friend found the car near midnight and reported her missing. ISP and the Morgan County Sheriff ran road checks. Thirty-six days later her body was found in a cornfield about 7 miles northeast of Martinsville; ISP says she was strangled with a shoelace. In 1978 police looked for a connection with the Mary Beth 'Pixie' Grismore case (per an Indianapolis Star article shown by The Deck). DNA evidence was preserved and is occasionally tested, with no match (cousin, via NBC). ISP said in 2023 the case remains under investigation.

cases.audioScript: On January fourth, 1978, twenty-year-old Bruce Moser left work early to pick up his wife, twenty-two-year-old Margaret, for an appointment in town. The high-school sweethearts lived in a mobile home on State Road 3, just north of the Wells and Blackford county line near Montpelier, with their toddler daughter, Kerri. When Bruce did not come to work for two days, his manager asked police to check on the family. Deputies found Bruce and Margaret dead. Both had been tied up and shot. Their little girl was alive, alone in the home, hungry and frightened, after about two days. Indiana State Police took over the case. Investigators later said they focused on one man, a truck driver whose route passed the Moser home, but he died before he could be questioned further, and he was never charged. DNA was collected at the scene and is still preserved, and an ISP captain said in 2021 he would not still be working the case if he did not think it could be solved. If someone ever told you they were involved, investigators want to hear from you.

cases.audioScript: On February twenty-second, 1978, Mary Beth Grismore, known to everyone as Pixie, was supposed to start a new life. The twenty-six-year-old mother of two had just remarried and was moving from her rural home near Marshall, in Parke County, Indiana, to join her husband in Iowa. Instead, she vanished, along with her car. A mechanic in nearby Rockville later told police he saw her car that morning with a man behind the wheel. He agreed to be hypnotized to help remember, and the FBI drew a composite sketch. In early May, police in Whitehall, Ohio, near Columbus, checked on an abandoned car in a Holiday Inn parking lot. Pixie's body was in the trunk. Many of her belongings, including oil paintings she had signed 'Pixie', a wall clock and fine china, were missing and have never turned up. Her case is on the cold-case lists of both the Indiana State Police and the Ohio Attorney General. If you ever came across a painting signed 'Pixie' or remember her car in February 1978, call the Indiana State Police or the FBI.

Household items, including oil paintings signed 'PIXIE', were missing from the car. A Rockville mechanic said he saw a man driving her car that morning; a composite sketch was produced (FBI, via The Deck). In 1978 police looked for links to the Ann Harmeier case (IN-053). The case is open in both states.

cases.audioScript: In November 1988, in the small city of Brazil, Indiana, thirty-two-year-old Ricky Mustard and his sixteen-year-old stepdaughter, Tonya Pickett, were shot and killed inside their home on West Pinckley Street. Tonya had been at a Northview High School dance that night. Their bodies were found just after one in the morning on November nineteenth, when Tonya's mother came home from work. For years the case went nowhere. Then, in 2002, the Indiana State Police assigned its cold case homicide team. Their work led to a special prosecutor, and in March 2008 a grand jury returned an indictment. But a judge ruled that nearly two hundred letters, a key part of the evidence, were hearsay and could not be used. The Court of Appeals agreed, and in 2012 the charges were dismissed. No one has been convicted. Ricky's son Shane was thirteen when he lost his father and stepsister. Now in his fifties, he calls police and reporters every November so the case is not forgotten. If you know something about that night in 1988, contact the Indiana State Police.

cases.audioScript: On November eleventh, 1981, fifteen-year-old Marie Bridget Patrick and a sixteen-year-old friend set out from Cincinnati, hoping to run away to Texas. They were hitchhiking, and a semi-truck driver picked them up. He told them his name was Bill. As they rolled west on Interstate 64 into southern Indiana, he began making sexual advances and threats. Near mile marker sixty-seven in Dubois County, the girls demanded to be let out. There was a struggle, and Marie was stabbed. In the chaos, Marie shoved her friend out of the door of the moving truck. Her friend survived with a minor injury. Marie could not get out. She was found dead about five miles farther down the interstate. The trucker has never been identified. Newspapers at the time described a white cab pulling a silver-gray trailer, and police even considered hypnosis to help with the description. More than forty years later, the Indiana State Police still list Marie's case as open. Somewhere, a man called Bill may have bragged about that night, or a company may remember a driver on I-64 that week.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of February twenty-fourth, 1987, ten-year-old Linda Weldy stepped off her school bus on West McClung Road in LaPorte, Indiana. The driver and other children watched her walk toward the family mailbox at the end of a long, curving gravel driveway that led to her home, hidden by trees. She never made it to the door. Linda loved fishing, riding her bike, and the TV show Mork and Mindy. Her mother was working a late factory shift and had no phone at home, so it was close to midnight before she learned her daughter was missing. Three weeks later, a farmer found Linda's body along an abandoned railroad line near Kingsbury, miles from home. She had been strangled. Over the years, LaPorte County detectives have developed persons of interest, but no one has ever been arrested. In 2014 the sheriff's office sent old and never-before-tested evidence to the Indiana State Police lab, hoping new DNA technology could finally point to her killer. If you saw anything on McClung Road that afternoon, LaPorte County detectives still want to hear from you.

cases.audioScript: In the summer of 1988, Keyla Weddel was getting ready for her twelfth year of teaching at Medora Elementary School, in a farming town of fewer than seven hundred people in Jackson County, Indiana. She was thirty-three, the mother of three small children, including twins, and she also worked part time at the county courthouse in Brownstown. Keyla lived in a mobile home behind her parents' house. She was last seen on the evening of August seventeenth. The next morning, her mother found her dead in her bedroom. She had been beaten. Police found no sign of forced entry, and nothing had been stolen. The killing changed Medora. People who had never locked their doors started locking them. Over thirty years, there have been countless tips and hundreds of interviews, and several detectives have worked the case. In 2018, the assigned Indiana State Police detective said some of Keyla's clothing and household items were at the state police lab for new testing. Her brother and sister are still waiting for justice. If you know what happened in Medora that night, call the Indiana State Police Versailles post.

cases.audioScript: On March twenty-ninth, 1993, nineteen-year-old Tricia Reitler, a freshman at Indiana Wesleyan University in Marion, took a break from writing a paper. She walked to a nearby Marsh supermarket, bought a soda and a magazine, and started back toward her dorm. She never arrived. cases.audioScript: On November sixth, 1997, thirteen-year-old Ricky Lane Thomas Junior called his cousin from his family's home in rural Bristow, in Perry County, Indiana. They had plans to go to Tell City, and Ricky wanted McDonald's. He said he would walk the mile or so to her house. Ricky was last seen walking along Oak Ridge Road with his two young hunting-dog puppies. He never arrived. Neither Ricky nor the puppies were ever seen again. He wasn't reported to police until the next day. Investigators searched extensively but found nothing. Indiana State Police say they believe Ricky's disappearance could be the result of a criminal act, and the detective assigned to the case said publicly that he believed Ricky had met with foul play. Ricky would be in his forties today. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progressed image, and Ricky has small scars on both cheeks that could help identify him. If you remember a boy with two puppies on Oak Ridge Road that November afternoon, please call the Indiana State Police Jasper post.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of June seventeenth, 2002, forty-six-year-old Nancy Lyons drove from her apartment in Carthage, Indiana, to nearby Rushville to pick up groceries and medicine. On her way home, she stopped at a rural intersection, County Road 700 West and 500 North in Rush County. No one knows why. A passerby found her red 1993 Nissan a few hours later. The engine was running, the trunk was open, a back tire was flat, and Nancy's belongings, including her cell phone, were still inside. Nancy was gone. Her family searched for months. In October, a farmer in Bartholomew County found human remains in his soybean field. They were Nancy's. She had died from a blow to the head. Nancy loved to sing and dance, stay up late talking, and spoil her nieces and nephews. Her sister Beverly started The Nancy Lyons Project, gathered hundreds of letters to state officials, and helped push for Molly's Law, which improved how Indiana handles missing-person cases. No one has been arrested. If you drove past that intersection that night, call the Indiana State Police.
cases.summary: Nancy Lyons, 46, of Carthage, was returning from Rushville on June 17, 2002, when she stopped at CR 700 W and CR 500 N in Rush County. Late that evening her red 1993 Nissan (Indiana plate 39A8348) was found running, unoccupied, trunk open, left rear tire flat, with her belongings inside. On Oct 2, 2002, her skeletal remains were found in a soybean field on CR 1000 E between CR 200 S and 300 S in Bartholomew County. Medical experts determined she died from a blow to the head. No suspects have been named and no arrests made. Her sister Beverly Tallent runs The Nancy Lyons Project and campaigned for Molly's Law (2007).

cases.audioScript: On October twenty-first, 2005, in the tiny LaGrange County community of Mongo, Indiana, someone came onto the rural property of Terry and Darleen Anderson and beat them both to death. Terry, fifty-nine, worked for a tree-service company and loved to hunt. He was found in his pole barn, where he had been working on a tractor. Darleen, fifty-seven, was close to retiring after thirty-five years at Kraft Foods in Kendallville. She was found on the couch, a bowl of popcorn beside her. There was no sign of forced entry. Investigators have said since 2011 that they believe they know who committed the crimes, but no charges have ever been filed, and some family members question that theory. Indiana State Police and the LaGrange County Sheriff still want to hear from anyone who saw a vehicle, heard something, or was told something about that night.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning hours of November twenty-first, 2016, fire tore through a house on East Columbia Street in Flora, a small town in Carroll County, Indiana. Inside were four sisters: Keyana Davis, eleven; Keyara Phillips, nine; Kerriele McDonald, seven; and Kionnie Welch, five. All four girls died. Their mother, Gaylin Rose, survived with injuries, and two police officers who rushed to help were also hurt. Investigators later determined the fire had been set on purpose. It was arson. Indiana State Police lead the case, with the FBI's Indianapolis office alongside them. The house was torn down in 2023, but the case was not set aside. In July 2025, state and federal agents went door to door in Flora again. And in November 2026, as the tenth anniversary approached, the FBI announced a reward of up to fifty thousand dollars. Its Indianapolis chief said plainly: this is not a cold case. The FBI says the girls' mother is a victim, not a suspect. If you saw, heard, or were told anything about that night, call 1-800-CALL-FBI, or the Indiana State Police.
cases.summary: Early on Nov 21, 2016, a fire at 103 E. Columbia St., Flora, killed sisters Keyana Davis (11), Keyara Phillips (9), Kerriele McDonald (7) and Kionnie Welch (5). The fire was determined to have been intentionally set (criminal case opened Feb 2017, per Carroll County Comet).
